brief.conference_theme: Shaping the future of urban forestry for greener cities and healthier communities
brief.panel_theme: Tree equity and nature prescriptions: trees as public health infrastructure

plan.summary: Find regional, budget-conscious panelists for a practitioner-focused discussion of tree equity and nature prescriptions as public health infrastructure in Washington, DC and Maryland. Favor rising and established speakers with evidence of prior presentations, and assemble complementary health, forestry, equity, and policy perspectives.
plan.location_focus: Washington, DC and Maryland; regional Mid-Atlantic if needed

angles: public health or urban forestry faculty at University of Maryland and University of the District of Columbia presenting research on tree canopy, health, or environmental justice
researchers at USDA Forest Service Northern Research Station and University of Maryland Extension who present on urban forestry or nature and health
urban forestry and parks staff at DC Department of Energy & Environment, DC Department of Parks and Recreation, and Maryland Department of Natural Resources who have presented on tree equity
community forestry or nature-prescription program leads at Casey Trees and local health systems in DC and Maryland with conference presentations
DC and Maryland government officials working on urban tree canopy, heat, environmental justice, or public health who have presented at regional planning or forestry events
policy researchers at Chesapeake Bay Foundation and regional planning organizations addressing tree canopy equity and community health

DC and Maryland founders or program leaders at urban forestry, green infrastructure, and nature-based health organizations who have spoken at U.S. Green Building Council National Capital Region or regional sustainability events
local landscape architecture and environmental consulting firm principals presenting on equitable urban canopy or nature-based public health interventions
community forestry and tree equity organizers at Casey Trees, Tree Baltimore, and Prince George's County environmental justice organizations with prior public presentations
leaders of DC and Maryland community health or parks nonprofits advancing nature prescriptions, green space access, or neighborhood tree planting who have presented at regional events
Washington-area reporters covering urban heat, public health, parks, and environmental justice at The Washington Post, DCist, and Maryland Matters who moderate public forums
DC and Maryland environmental journalists or science communicators who have hosted panels at Chesapeake Bay or regional conservation conferences

cards.name: Jennifer D. Roberts
cards.job_title: Associate Professor, Department of Kinesiology; Co-Founder and Co-Director, NatureRx@UMD; Founder and Director, PHOEBE Laboratory
cards.organization: University of Maryland School of Public Health
cards.could_speak_on: How green-space access, structural inequities, and public-health research can inform nature-prescription programs and equitable urban forestry.
talk_ideas: Green-space benefits and nature prescriptions in community health
Measuring health equity impacts of the built and natural environment
Addressing structural inequities in access to urban green space
cards.bio: Jennifer D. Roberts is a tenured associate professor in the University of Maryland School of Public Health’s Department of Kinesiology. She founded and directs the PHOEBE Laboratory and co-founded and co-directs NatureRx@UMD, and her scholarship examines how built, social, and natural environments affect health.
cards.why_fit: Direct local fit for the panel’s nature-prescription and health-equity focus, with leadership of a university NatureRx initiative.
cards.fit_reason: Exceptional geographic and subject fit; however, no public speaking appearance was confirmed in the pages read.

cards.name: Michelle C. Kondo
cards.organization: USDA Forest Service, Northern Research Station
cards.could_speak_on: Research evidence linking urban trees, community-led greening, nature prescriptions, and public health, including lessons from Philadelphia’s tree-canopy goals.
talk_ideas: Nature prescriptions: evidence and research opportunities
Public-health outcomes of community-based urban forestry
Connecting canopy goals with equitable access and health
cards.bio: Michelle Kondo is a research social scientist with the USDA Forest Service’s Northern Research Station. Her work includes research on nature prescriptions, health impacts of tree-canopy goals, and community-based urban greening.
cards.why_fit: Strong research match for the panel’s public-health infrastructure frame, with a verified webinar on community-based urban forestry and Philadelphia canopy goals.

past_speaking.event: Urban Forest Connections webinar: Methods and Public Health Impacts of Community-Based Urban Forestry Efforts

notable_work: Nature Prescriptions for Health: A Review of Evidence and Research Opportunities
Health impact assessment of Philadelphia’s 2025 tree canopy cover goals
cards.fit_reason: Excellent thematic match and verified webinar appearance, though based outside the requested DC/Maryland region.

cards.name: Meghan Avolio
cards.job_title: Associate Professor, Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences
cards.could_speak_on: What Baltimore’s street-tree patterns reveal about environmental injustice, alongside ecological research on how urban environments shape plant communities.
talk_ideas: Baltimore street trees and the legacy of housing policy
Urban plant communities and neighborhood environments
Using ecological evidence to understand inequity in urban forests
cards.bio: Meghan Avolio is an associate professor in Johns Hopkins University’s Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences. Her research examines plants in cities and grasslands, including how urban environments affect plant populations and communities.
cards.why_fit: A Baltimore-based ecologist whose work includes research on street-tree communities and race-based housing policy, bringing a locally grounded ecological perspective.

past_speaking.event: Horticulture Seminar Series: Plant community assembly in urban areas

notable_work: Current Street Tree Communities Reflect Race-based Housing Policy and Modern Attempts to Remedy Environmental Injustice
cards.fit_reason: Strong regional and tree-equity research fit with a confirmed seminar presentation, though her work is more ecological than clinical public health.

cards.name: J.T. Bowers
cards.could_speak_on: Maryland’s urban-forestry programs and how state partnerships can connect tree canopy expansion with public health and environmental justice.
talk_ideas: Expanding urban forestry as public-health infrastructure
State support for tree canopy in underserved communities
Building local capacity through urban-forestry partnerships
cards.bio: J.T. Bowers serves as Deputy Director of the Maryland Forest Service, leading statewide forestry policy, strategic initiatives, and agency modernization efforts. His work includes expanding urban and community forestry programs and integrating forestry into public-health and environmental-justice policy.
credentials: Master of Science in Conservation Ecology
cards.why_fit: A Maryland state-practice perspective closely matches the regional audience and panel’s focus on connecting trees, community access, and health.

past_speaking.event: 2026 Urban Tree Summit: “The Expanding Mandate of Maryland’s Urban Forests”

notable_work: Expanded urban and community forestry programs

links.label: 2026 Urban Tree Summit agenda and speaker information

cards.fit_reason: Directly relevant Maryland agency leader with documented experience in urban forestry, underserved-community canopy work, public health, and a recent regional summit presentation.

cards.name: Leslie Berckes
cards.could_speak_on: The workforce and operational realities of urban forestry that shape cities’ ability to sustain tree-care and canopy programs.
talk_ideas: The people and systems needed to manage urban forests
Building the next generation of urban foresters
Practical challenges in municipal tree planting and care
cards.bio: Leslie Berckes is Executive Director of the Urban and Community Forestry Society. Her work and public appearances address the professional community that makes daily tree planting and care decisions, including workforce development and the varied demands of urban forestry.
cards.why_fit: Offers a practitioner and workforce-systems angle relevant to putting urban forestry into practice, but is based outside the requested DC/Maryland region and has less direct evidence on tree equity or nature prescriptions.

past_speaking.event: The Municipal Arborist podcast: Leslie Berckes and the Urban & Community Forestry Society
Internet of Nature podcast: Where have all the young urban foresters gone, and how to get them back?

cards.fit_reason: Confirmed practitioner leader with multiple relevant speaking appearances; lower regional fit and limited direct evidence linking her work to health or equity.

cards.name: Earl Eutsler
cards.job_title: Associate Director for Urban Forestry Division
cards.could_speak_on: How data-driven public-tree management can target resources across neighborhoods and sustain urban canopy as public infrastructure.
talk_ideas: Using tree-service data to direct resources where they are most needed
Building community engagement into city tree-planting programs
Managing urban tree canopy for resilient, healthier neighborhoods
cards.bio: Earl Eutsler is Associate Director for DDOT’s Urban Forestry Division, where he has served since 2004. His work has included developing data-driven approaches to protecting and increasing Washington, DC’s tree canopy and improving the division’s service delivery.
credentials: Master’s degree in environmental science and policy, Johns Hopkins University
cards.why_fit: A directly relevant regional government practitioner who can explain how public agencies manage street trees, prioritize service and planting, and engage communities. His documented 2021 practitioner lecture also meets the brief’s preference for prior speakers.

past_speaking.event: Wetmore Visiting Practitioner Lecture: “Urban Forestry in DC: The Simple Act of Keeping Track,” University of Illinois Department of Urban and Regional Planning

notable_work: Led DDOT Urban Forestry Division work on data-driven tree-canopy protection and growth.
DDOT’s urban forestry program has focused on expanding community engagement and installing thousands of trees annually, according to his American Planning Association profile.
cards.fit_reason: Current DC urban-forestry leadership, strong regional relevance, and a confirmed prior practitioner lecture.

cards.name: Abel Olivo
cards.could_speak_on: How community-led tree planting and environmental education can expand access to urban nature and connect tree equity with healthier communities.
talk_ideas: Building community capacity for equitable urban tree programs
Engaging Latino and Spanish-speaking communities in watershed and tree initiatives
Training local ambassadors to support tree planting and stewardship
cards.bio: Abel Olivo is Co-Founder and Executive Director of Defensores de la Cuenca, which engages Latino and Spanish-speaking communities in watershed-related issues. The organization has received support for tree planting and training community tree ambassadors in Prince George’s County and surrounding areas.
credentials: Serves on the Stakeholders Advisory Committee of the Chesapeake Executive Council
cards.why_fit: His leadership connects regional tree planting with community engagement, environmental education, and access to nature—an especially relevant perspective for a practitioner audience discussing tree equity as public-health infrastructure.
notable_work: Defensores de la Cuenca’s urban tree planting and community tree ambassador work in Prince George’s County and surrounding areas

links.label: Defensores de la Cuenca team profile
Chesapeake Bay Trust feature on urban tree work
Maryland Outdoor Recreation Summit speaker profile

cards.fit_reason: Regional nonprofit co-founder with verified tree-planting work and public appearances, bringing a direct community-engagement perspective to the panel.

cards.name: Erin Douglas
cards.job_title: Freelance climate, energy, and environment journalist
cards.could_speak_on: She can connect environmental-health reporting and climate resilience to practical questions about trees as neighborhood health infrastructure.

Looking for people who would make great panels together…
Suggested 2 panel(s): Can Trees Be Prescribed?; From Canopy Gaps to Health Gains

panels.title: Can Trees Be Prescribed?
panels.question: How can cities turn evidence on nature, health, and unequal tree access into practical public-health infrastructure?

members.name: Jennifer D. Roberts
members.angle: Connects green-space access, structural inequities, and public-health research to nature-prescription programs.

members.name: J.T. Bowers
members.angle: Brings Maryland’s urban-forestry programs and state partnerships into the discussion of canopy expansion, health, and environmental justice.

members.name: Earl Eutsler
members.angle: Offers a city-management perspective on using public-tree data to target neighborhood resources and sustain canopy.

members.name: Abel Olivo
members.angle: Brings community-led tree planting and environmental education experience focused on expanding access to urban nature.

moderator.name: Aman Azhar
moderator.angle: Adds a Maryland-focused environmental-justice reporting lens and experience moderating public discussions.

why_together: Brings research, state and city implementation, and community-led stewardship to one practical question.
Their perspectives span the health case for nature prescriptions, the systems for delivering trees, and how communities participate.
The local and regional focus fits the Washington, DC/Maryland audience.
panels.tension: How can public agencies use data and health evidence to direct investment while ensuring community priorities and stewardship shape where and how tree programs are delivered?
panels.balance_note: A regional mix of academic, state and city policy, and community-based leadership; all members are established, with a journalist moderator.

panels.title: From Canopy Gaps to Health Gains
panels.question: What does it take to turn evidence about unequal tree cover and public health into lasting, equitable urban-forestry programs?

members.name: Michelle C. Kondo
members.angle: Brings research on links among urban trees, community-led greening, nature prescriptions, and public health.

members.name: Meghan Avolio
members.angle: Uses Baltimore street-tree patterns and urban plant ecology to show how neighborhood environments reflect inequity.

members.name: Leslie Berckes
members.angle: Highlights the workforce and operational systems cities need to sustain tree care and canopy programs.

members.name: J.T. Bowers
members.angle: Offers a Maryland program and partnership perspective on expanding urban forestry in underserved communities.

moderator.name: Sarah Kaplan
moderator.angle: Can frame the discussion around climate impacts on communities and moderate a cross-disciplinary conversation about trees, heat, and health.

why_together: Pairs evidence on health and neighborhood tree patterns with the practical challenge of maintaining trees over time.
Connects regional equity questions to workforce capacity and state-level partnership approaches.
The panel can move from identifying canopy gaps to discussing what it takes to close them sustainably.
panels.tension: Research can identify health benefits and inequities, but durable improvements also depend on workforce, maintenance capacity, and choices about how public programs allocate resources.
panels.balance_note: Two academic researchers and two forestry practitioners bring complementary evidence and implementation perspectives; the moderator adds climate communication experience.
